```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
```

# Problem 1

```{r p1_import}
data("ny_noaa")

noaa_missing =
  ny_noaa |>
  summarize(across(prcp:tmin, \(x) mean(is.na(x))))

n_stations_noaa = n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)
n_stations_no_temp =
  ny_noaa |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarize(no_temp = all(is.na(tmax))) |>
  filter(no_temp) |>
  nrow()
```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains daily weather records from NOAA weather stations in New York State. It has `r format(nrow(ny_noaa), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns, with one row per station per day, covering `r n_stations_noaa` stations from `r min(ny_noaa$date)` to `r max(ny_noaa$date)`. Key variables are the station `id`, the `date`, precipitation (`prcp`, tenths of mm), snowfall (`snow`, mm), snow depth (`snwd`, mm), and maximum and minimum temperature (`tmax`, `tmin`, tenths of degrees C; stored as character). Missing data is a major issue: `r round(noaa_missing$prcp * 100, 1)`% of `prcp`, `r round(noaa_missing$snow * 100, 1)`% of `snow`, `r round(noaa_missing$snwd * 100, 1)`% of `snwd`, and about `r round(noaa_missing$tmax * 100, 1)`% of `tmax` and `tmin` are missing. Many stations only record precipitation and snow; `r n_stations_no_temp` of the `r n_stations_noaa` stations never report a temperature.

```{r p1_clean}
noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), convert = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

noaa_df |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Snowfall (mm)", "Number of days"))
```

I split `date` into integer `year`, `month`, and `day` variables, converted `tmax` and `tmin` from character to numeric and from tenths of degrees C to degrees C, and converted `prcp` from tenths of mm to mm. Snowfall and snow depth are already in mm and were left unchanged.

For snowfall, the most common value by far is 0: most days in New York have no snow, and snow is impossible for much of the year. The next most common value is `NA`, reflecting the missingness above. Among nonzero values, the most common are 25, 13, 51, and 76 mm. These correspond to 1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches, which suggests snowfall is usually measured in (half) inches by observers and then converted to mm.

```{r p1_jan_jul, message = FALSE}
noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
  mutate(month = factor(month, levels = c(1, 7), labels = c("January", "July"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = id), alpha = .15) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "darkorange") +
  facet_wrap(~ month, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Average max temperature by station, January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average max temperature (°C)",
    caption = "Each grey line is one station; the orange line is a smooth across stations"
  )
```

Each grey line is one station's average daily maximum temperature in that month and year. As expected, January is much colder than July (roughly 0°C versus 27°C on average), and January temperatures vary more across stations and years. Within each month, stations move up and down together from year to year, so most variation comes from year-to-year weather (e.g. a cold January in 1994 and warm Januaries in 1990, 2002, and 2006) rather than from station differences. There is no strong long-term trend over this 30-year period. A few stations stand out as outliers, such as a station with an average January max of about -13°C in 1982, and a station with an unusually cold July in 1988 (about 14°C, far below all other stations).

```{r p1_tmax_snow, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
tmax_tmin_p =
  noaa_df |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10") +
  labs(
    title = "Max vs min daily temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"))

snow_p =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges(scale = 1.5, fill = "lightblue", alpha = .7) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall between 0 and 100 mm",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  )

tmax_tmin_p + snow_p
```

Because there are over a million days with both temperatures recorded, a scatterplot would mostly show overplotting, so the left panel uses a 2D binned plot with counts on a log scale. Maximum and minimum temperatures are strongly positively related, and most days fall in a dense band just above the line `tmax = tmin`. A small number of points have `tmax` below `tmin` or extreme values (e.g. 60°C), which are likely recording errors.

The right panel shows the distribution of snowfall between 0 and 100 mm in each year. The distributions are very similar across years: they are multimodal, with peaks at about 13, 25, 51, and 76 mm, matching the half-inch and inch values noted above. The median nonzero snowfall in this range is 25 mm in every year. From about 2006 onward, a slightly larger share of values are small (roughly 20% below 10 mm, compared with about 15% in earlier years), and the number of snowfall records also increases, possibly reflecting new stations or changes in measurement practice.

# Problem 2

```{r p2_import, message = FALSE}
# The first 4 rows of the covariate file describe the codes, so skip them
covar_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")
    )
  )

accel_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_df =
  inner_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn") |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(minute = as.integer(minute))
```

The covariate file has four rows of code descriptions above the header, so I skipped them. I removed participants younger than 21 and those missing any demographic variable (BMI or education), then recoded `sex` and `education` from numeric codes to factors whose levels are in a natural order (education from lowest to highest). The accelerometer file has one row per participant and one column per minute (`min1`–`min1440`); every participant in it also appears in the covariate file. After joining the two by `seqn`, I pivoted the minute columns to long format so that `minute` (1–1440, starting at midnight) and `mims` are variables. The final dataset has `r format(nrow(nhanes_df), big.mark = ",")` rows (one per participant-minute) for `r n_distinct(nhanes_df$seqn)` participants, with variables `r paste0("\x60", names(nhanes_df), "\x60", collapse = ", ")`.

```{r p2_table}
covar_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Education", "Men", "Women"))
```

```{r p2_age_plot}
covar_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = sex),
    position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = .15, dodge.width = .75),
    alpha = .5,
    size = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution by education and sex",
    x = "Education",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Men and women are roughly balanced in the "less than high school" (27 vs 28) and "more than high school" (56 vs 59) groups, but there are more men than women with a high school equivalent education (35 vs 23). The "more than high school" group is the largest for both sexes. Participants with more than high school education tend to be younger (median age in the low 40s for both sexes) than those with less education. In the high school equivalent group, women are noticeably older than men (median about 62 vs 53), while in the "less than high school" group the age distributions of men and women are similar and skew older (median around 60). These age differences matter when comparing activity across education groups, since activity tends to decline with age.

```{r p2_total_activity, message = FALSE}
total_activity_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims), .groups = "drop")

total_activity_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity vs age",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

In all three education groups, total daily activity generally declines with age. In the more than high school group, women have higher total activity than men across nearly the whole age range, and both decline mainly after about age 60. In the high school equivalent group, women are clearly more active than men from their 20s to about age 55, after which the two sexes are similar. In the less than high school group, the smooths cross: women are more active in their 20s and 30s, men are somewhat more active around ages 55–70, and both sexes show the steepest overall decline with age in this group. The smooths are based on relatively few participants per panel, so the wiggles (for example, the bump around age 40 for high school equivalent women) should not be over-interpreted.

```{r p2_time_course, message = FALSE, fig.width = 10}
nhanes_df |>
  mutate(hour = minute / 60) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = seqn), alpha = .05) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 6)) +
  labs(
    title = "24-hour activity time course by education and sex",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Each faint line is one participant's minute-by-minute activity, and the bold lines are smooths for men and women. In every education group, activity follows the same daily pattern: it is lowest overnight (around 2–5 am), rises sharply in the morning between about 6 and 9 am, stays high through midday and afternoon, and declines in the evening. The individual time courses are very noisy, with frequent spikes above 50 MIMS. The smooths show that women are slightly more active than men during the day in the high school equivalent and more than high school groups, while men and women are similar during the day in the less than high school group (where men are slightly more active late at night). Differences across education levels are small overall compared with the variation within each group.

# Problem 3

```{r p3_import, message = FALSE}
citi_files = list.files("data/citibike", pattern = "\\.csv\\.zip$", full.names = TRUE)

# Month and year come from the file names, e.g. "Jan 2020 Citi.csv.zip"
citi_df =
  map(citi_files, read_csv) |>
  set_names(basename(citi_files)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "file") |>
  separate(file, into = c("month", "year"), sep = " ", extra = "drop", convert = TRUE) |>
  rename(weekday = weekdays, duration_min = duration, rider_type = member_casual) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("Jan", "July"), labels = c("January", "July")),
    weekday = factor(
      weekday,
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type,
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"),
      labels = c("Classic", "Electric")
    ),
    rider_type = factor(rider_type, levels = c("member", "casual"), labels = c("Member", "Casual"))
  ) |>
  relocate(ride_id, year, month, weekday)
```

The four files (January and July of 2020 and 2024) share the same columns, so I read them all, stacked them, and created `year` and `month` variables from the file names. I renamed variables to be clearer (`weekday`, `duration_min`, `rider_type`) and converted `month`, `weekday`, `rideable_type`, and `rider_type` to factors with a sensible ordering (e.g. Monday to Sunday). The resulting dataset has `r format(nrow(citi_df), big.mark = ",")` rides (one per row) and `r ncol(citi_df)` variables: `r paste0("\x60", names(citi_df), "\x60", collapse = ", ")`. Ride durations are in minutes and range from `r round(min(citi_df$duration_min), 1)` to `r round(max(citi_df$duration_min), 1)` minutes, with a median of `r round(median(citi_df$duration_min), 1)`. The only missing values are `r sum(is.na(citi_df$start_station_name))` missing start stations and `r sum(is.na(citi_df$end_station_name))` missing end stations; these rides are kept, since their other information is still valid.

```{r p3_rides_table}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month, rider_type) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rider_type, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.character(year),
    Total = Member + Casual,
    pct_casual = scales::percent(Casual / Total, accuracy = .1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Member", "Casual", "Total", "% casual"),
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
  )
```

Ridership grew substantially from 2020 to 2024: the number of rides in this 1% sample increased by about 50% in January and more than doubled in July. In both years, there are many more rides in July than in January, reflecting the seasonal nature of cycling. Members take the large majority of rides in every month. Casual riders make up a much larger share of rides in summer (about a quarter in July) than in winter (about 8–11% in January), suggesting that casual use is more weather-dependent and possibly driven by tourists and leisure trips.

```{r p3_top_stations}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |>
  count(start_station_name, name = "n_rides") |>
  slice_max(n_rides, n = 5) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Starting station", "Number of rides"))
```

The most popular starting stations in July 2024 are all in Manhattan, mostly along the west side and around Chelsea, Union Square, and Lower Manhattan, with Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers at the top.

```{r p3_median_duration}
citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekday) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration_min), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekday, y = median_duration, color = year, group = year)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by day of week, month, and year",
    x = "Day of week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Median rides are longer in July than in January in both years, and longer on weekends (Saturday and Sunday) than on weekdays, consistent with more leisurely riding in summer and on weekends, compared with shorter commuting trips on weekdays. Rides in 2024 are shorter than in 2020 for every day and month, and the difference is largest in July 2020, when median rides were about 13–17 minutes compared with about 9–11 minutes in July 2024. One possible explanation is that July 2020 was during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many people rode for recreation rather than commuting, while the larger number of electric bikes in 2024 also makes trips faster. The weekend effect is weakest in January 2024, where Sunday rides are not longer than weekday rides.

```{r p3_duration_2024}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type, y = duration_min, fill = rider_type)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = .5, position = position_dodge(width = .8)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = .15,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    position = position_dodge(width = .8),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of ride duration in 2024",
    x = "Bike type",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes, log scale)",
    fill = "Rider type"
  )
```

Ride durations are right-skewed, so they are shown on a log scale. Membership status has the largest effect: casual riders take longer rides than members for both bike types and in both months (e.g. median casual rides are roughly 9–16 minutes, compared with about 7–9 minutes for members), and their durations are more spread out. This is consistent with members using bikes for regular, direct trips such as commuting, while casual riders ride more for leisure. Rides are somewhat longer in July than in January, especially for casual riders. For casual riders, electric bike rides are shorter than classic bike rides, likely because electric bikes are faster; for members, bike type makes little difference in January and electric rides are slightly longer in July.
